guideTitle: Best Space Heaters with Remote and App Control (2026)
metaTitle: Best Space Heaters with Remote and App Control
metaDescription: Five Wi-Fi space heaters that also ship with a handheld remote, compared by app features, voice support and noise so you can control warmth from anywhere.
expertTake: The DREO smart wall heater is the best pick for anyone who wants real scheduling, because it combines a remote, an app and a 41 to 95 degree range in one cabinet. The SereneLife is the value choice, adding Wi-Fi to a conventional ceramic body. If you only change the heat from your chair and never from your phone, a plain remote model is cheaper and has fewer things that can break.
introParagraphs: App control sounds like a gimmick until you want the bedroom warm before you get home or you realise the heater has been running in an empty room all afternoon. Wi-Fi turns a space heater into a device you can check, schedule and switch off from your phone.

The catch is that these heaters add a radio, a cloud account and a setup process. This guide looks at heaters that keep a handheld remote as well, so a dropped connection never leaves you without control.

products.name: DREO Smart Wall Heater 1500W with Remote, App, 120° Sweep and ECO Mode
products.description:
A heater that hangs on the wall changes the app question, because nobody moves it and nobody trips over it. This DREO lists a 120 degree sweep, which is wide enough to cover a bedroom from one fixed spot, plus scheduling so the heating hours match your routine. The adjustable temperature range runs from 41 to 95 degrees, which also makes it useful as a frost guard.

Scheduling is the app feature that actually changes behaviour. You set a block, the heater warms the room before you arrive and the ECO mode trims power once the target is reached. The remote remains for the moments when the phone is across the house.

Because it is wall-mounted, installation is a half-hour job with anchors, and it has no fan base to collect dust. Against the SereneLife floor unit it costs more and needs a fixed location, but it is the one where the app earns its keep. Best for a bedroom or a home office you use every day. One practical note on a wall heater: put it where the airflow is not blocked by a bed, a desk or a curtain, because a unit mounted high and sweeping 120 degrees loses its advantage if the louvres face a wardrobe. Leave the area beneath it clear as well, since warm air rises from the outlet and anything hanging below will collect it.
products.bestFor: Daily-use bedrooms and offices where scheduling saves effort.
pros: 120 degree sweep from a fixed wall position
Schedule heating hours from the app
41 to 95 degree range doubles as a frost guard
cons: Needs a wall mount and a nearby outlet
Costs more than a floor heater

products.name: SereneLife Smart 1500W Ceramic Heater with Wi-Fi, Remote and 12-Hour Timer
products.description:
The SereneLife takes a conventional 1500W PTC ceramic heater and adds a Wi-Fi radio, a remote and a 12 hour timer, so it behaves like an ordinary heater first and a smart one second. That ordering matters: if the app is down or the router is rebooting, the thermostat and remote still run the machine.

The floor-standing body trades the DREO's wall position for portability, which means you can carry it between rooms but must re-aim it each time. The listing mentions overheat protection and tip-over safety, so basic cutouts are present.

Setup is the typical smart-appliance exercise: download the app, join a 2.4 GHz network and name the device. Keep the remote in reach, since it is the fallback. Compared with the FLANUR towers, this unit is shorter and simpler and suits a smaller room. Because the app and the timer both live in this one body, test the timer once from the app and once from the remote when you set it up, so you know which command wins if they ever disagree. A heater that has a thermostat, a remote and an app has three ways to be set to different targets, and finding that out on a cold night is unpleasant.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want smart features on a familiar ceramic body.
pros: Works as a normal heater if Wi-Fi drops
cons: Shorter body covers less floor than a tower

products.name: ROVSUN 24-Inch Oscillating Tower Heater with Remote and App, 1500W
products.description:
Two PTC stones inside a 24 inch tower give the ROVSUN a taller heating surface than a squat desktop unit, and the listing frames it as whole-room warming with remote and app control. The tower shape fits a corner and the oscillation spreads the output across the room.

The point of a tower is footprint: a narrow base uses little floor. The price of that shape is stability, so it belongs on a hard surface away from foot traffic. The app lets you start the room warming from a sofa upstairs or from the office.

Expect to update the app occasionally and to reconnect it if the router changes. A clean intake and a monthly plug check are the usual care. Beside the DREO wall unit it is more portable, and beside the FLANUR large-room tower it is a step simpler. It suits a living room or a larger bedroom. The two PTC stones are worth a thought for longevity: a ceramic plate has no filament to burn out, so the parts most likely to fail over several winters are the fan bearing, the oscillation motor and the Wi-Fi board rather than the element. That is a good reason to keep the remote working as well.
products.bestFor: Living rooms and large bedrooms wanting a tower with app control.
pros: Dual PTC stones in a 24 inch tower
Oscillation spreads output across the room
cons: Tall body needs a hard flat floor
App updates and reconnects add occasional chores

products.name: FLANUR 1500W PTC Smart Heater with Voice, Remote and App Control

specList.label: Use note
specList.value: Marketed for quiet sleep and focus

products.description:
Voice support is the angle on this FLANUR: the listing lists voice control alongside the app and a remote, so you can speak a command from a smart speaker instead of reaching for the phone. A 1500W PTC element supplies the heat and the maker pitches it at large rooms and quiet work or sleep.

Voice and app control rely on the same cloud connection, so expect a short delay on each command and an occasional dropped link. The remote is the dependable path when the connection is slow. A large-room claim should be read against the 10 watts per square foot rule: 1500W is a good match for about 150 square feet of well-insulated space.

Plan on a short setup, a name for the device and a firmware update or two. Against the other FLANUR model below, it lists no decibel figure, so it is the better choice for a living room than a bedroom. If you do use voice, learn the exact phrases the assistant accepts, because a heater that responds only to a rigid command wording quickly gets abandoned for the remote. Name the device something distinctive, so a request for the bedroom heater does not trigger the one in the lounge.
products.bestFor: Smart-speaker households who like to speak commands.
pros: Voice, app and remote all supported
Works as a conventional heater offline
cons: No decibel figure on the listing
Voice commands lag on a slow connection

products.name: FLANUR Smart Large-Room Heater, Wi-Fi, Voice and Remote, 23dB Fan
products.description:
Smart control is only useful if the heater does not irritate you the rest of the time, and this FLANUR lists a fan as quiet as 23dB, the lowest figure in this guide. It combines Wi-Fi, voice and a remote with an ECO thermostat and three heat modes.

An ECO mode paired with a schedule from the app is the practical benefit: you can set it to run for a few hours and let the thermostat decide how hard to work. At such a low noise level, it is the one in the group you could comfortably use in a bedroom.

Like the other FLANUR, it relies on a cloud connection, so keep the remote handy. Clean the intake each month and replace the remote battery each autumn. It suits bedrooms and quiet studies where the app is a convenience, not the whole point. The quiet fan also lets you hear the thermostat cycle, which is a useful clue: if the heater clicks on and off every few minutes, the target is set too close to the room temperature, and a slightly lower number will give longer, calmer cycles.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms and studies that want the quietest smart heater here.
pros: Listed fan noise as low as 23dB
cons: Relies on a cloud connection for app features
Large-room claim needs insulation to hold

buyingCriteria.criterion: Remote plus app, not app alone
buyingCriteria.explanation: An app-only heater is a liability when the router restarts or the cloud service is down. All five heaters here keep a handheld remote, and the SereneLife behaves like a normal heater with the thermostat. Treat the remote as the primary control and the app as an extra layer.

Look for scheduling, a temperature readout and remote on-off. The DREO wall heater adds scheduling and a 41 to 95 degree range, which matters. An app that only turns the heater on and off is no better than a smart plug, and plugging a heater into a smart plug is a poor idea.

Many smart heaters connect only to a 2.4 GHz network. If your router merges bands or hides the 2.4 GHz option, setup can fail. Read the listing for the band, and keep the router near the heater's location for the first pairing.
An app encourages you to run the heater while you sleep, so fan noise matters. The FLANUR at 23dB is the quietest listed here. Models without a figure are likely louder.

The DREO wall heater hangs in one place, so the app schedule always heats the same space. Floor units like the SereneLife and ROVSUN move, which means the schedule applies to wherever you put them. Decide whether the heater will stay put.

A smart heater creates an account and a link to a vendor cloud. Check that the heater still works with the remote if you decide not to connect it. All five here do, and you can leave the radio unused.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control layers
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked that each heater keeps a handheld remote and a panel in addition to the app. The SereneLife and the DREO wall heater both keep clear fallbacks. A smart heater with no offline control would have been excluded.

howWeEvaluated.title: App usefulness
howWeEvaluated.description: We read what the app can do beyond switching on. The DREO wall heater lists scheduling and a wide temperature range, which ranked it first. Voice-only extras ranked lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: A scheduled heater runs while you sleep, so we compared stated decibel figures. The FLANUR at 23dB set the benchmark. Models without a figure were scored cautiously.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup realism
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted the friction of pairing, such as 2.4 GHz requirements and account creation. The SereneLife and ROVSUN are straightforward on that front.

howWeEvaluated.title: Body and placement
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each heater to a placement: a wall unit for fixed rooms, a tower for a living room corner and a short floor unit for a spare room.

cards.label: Wall mount
cards.text: The DREO wall heater stays in one place, so schedules always heat the same space. It leaves floor clear and has no base to tip. You need an outlet at the right spot and a few anchors.

cards.label: Floor standing
cards.text: The SereneLife, ROVSUN and both FLANUR units move between rooms. They can be tipped, so a hard, flat spot matters, and the schedule follows whichever room you put them in.

howToChoose.note: Pick the wall unit if the room is fixed and daily; pick floor units if you want flexibility.

ECO thermostat and a quiet fan

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A schedule that starts before you arrive, a thermostat that stops at target and a stable Wi-Fi link. Remember the heater needs a clear 3 feet around it while unattended.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DREO wall heater is the best fit because it holds a schedule and hangs out of reach. The ROVSUN tower can pre-warm a living room if it stands on a hard floor.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You will use schedules daily or want the heater out of the way. The DREO wall heater justifies its price with automation.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only want to turn the heater on from your phone occasionally. The SereneLife adds Wi-Fi at the lowest cost here.

maintenance.why: Smart heaters drift out of date and lose pairing. A quick update before winter avoids a cold surprise.
The remote is your fallback. Keep a spare coin cell nearby.
Dust slows the fan and can trigger the overheat cutout.
Scheduled heaters run unattended, so a warm plug is a stronger warning. Never use an extension cord.
A new network name or password breaks the link. Re-run setup near the heater.

faq.q: Is it safe to schedule a heater while I am away?
faq.a: Only for short periods and with 3 feet of clear space. A schedule starts the heater when you are not there to see a problem. Use it to pre-warm before arriving, not to run all day.

faq.q: What if my Wi-Fi goes down?
faq.a: All five heaters keep a remote and a panel, so you can still operate them locally. The SereneLife behaves like a normal heater with its thermostat. Schedules may pause until the link returns, so confirm what each unit does after a power cut before you rely on it for an automatic morning warm-up. Some heaters resume their last setting, others wait for a button press.

faq.q: Do I need a smart plug instead?
faq.a: No. A smart plug cannot read temperature, and heaters should be plugged directly into the wall. A built-in app lets the heater regulate itself properly.
The FLANUR smart heater lists as low as 23dB. Others do not publish a figure. Wall-mounted units like the DREO have no base rattle.
It can, by switching the heater off when you leave and starting it only before you arrive. A 1500W heater draws 1.5 kWh each hour on high, so avoiding idle hours adds up.

faq.q: Why will my heater not connect?
faq.a: Most smart heaters accept only 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. If your router merges bands, split them temporarily and move closer during pairing. Check the listing for the supported band.
